prompt: A team has 4,000 tests, all written after the features they cover. Does it practise TDD?

choices.text: Yes: a suite that large is what TDD means
choices.why: The suite is a by-product of TDD, not its definition. A large suite written afterwards is test-last.

choices.text: No: in TDD each test is written before the code it drives
choices.why: Right. TDD is a way of writing the code, with the failing test first; the count of tests says nothing about the order.

choices.text: Only if the coverage report shows 100 per cent of lines run
choices.why: Coverage measures what the tests run, not when they were written. Test-last suites reach full coverage too.

prompt: Put one turn of the cycle in order.
items: Write one test for the next behaviour
Run it and see it fail for the expected reason
Write the least code that makes it pass
Improve names and structure with every test green
trap: Tidying before the test passes mixes two questions; the refactor step comes only after green.

prompt: Why does the method insist on watching a new test fail before writing any code for it?

choices.text: Because a failing run is faster than a passing one
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; both runs take a fraction of a second.

choices.text: A test never seen failing might not be testing anything at all
choices.why: Right. Until it has been red, there is no evidence it can tell working code from broken code.

choices.text: Because unittest refuses to run a test that has never failed before
choices.why: unittest keeps no history of runs; it runs whatever it collects.

choices.text: So that the commit history shows a red build before every green one
choices.why: The red run happens on your machine, in seconds; nobody commits it.

prompt: The first green version of fines.py is return 150. What has it already achieved?

choices.text: Nothing; it is a placeholder to delete before the real work
choices.why: It has done real work: the test is known to run and the interface is decided.

choices.text: It computes the fine correctly for every book returned three days late
choices.why: True of three days late and of nothing else, which is why the next test exists.

choices.text: The test is proved to run, and the name and arguments are fixed
choices.why: Right. Seen red then green, the test is known to run, and the call shape is decided before the formula.

prompt: The first run ends in ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fines'. How does the lesson read that?

choices.text: As a red run that fails for exactly the reason the test expected
choices.why: Right. The test describes code that does not exist yet; Beck counts this as a failing test, as Java would count a compile error.

choices.text: As a broken setup to repair before the cycle can start
choices.why: Python and unittest worked perfectly; the missing module is the point of the test.

choices.text: As a sign the test was written too early, before the module
choices.why: Before the module is exactly when TDD writes it.

prompt: unittest skipped a method called three_days_late_costs_150_cents, because its name lacks the prefix ___ .
In the lesson, what made return 150 give way to a formula?

choices.text: A code review that rejected the constant
choices.why: No reviewer was needed; a test did the rejecting.

choices.text: A second test the constant could not pass
choices.why: Right. 150 and 50 cannot both come from one constant, so the simplest code passing both is the general rule.

choices.text: The refactor step, which replaces every fake with real code
choices.why: Refactoring changes structure, never behaviour; turning 150 into a formula changed what fine returns for one day late.

choices.text: The first test, run a second time with -v so it names the case
choices.why: Running the same test again cannot fail a constant that already passed it.

prompt: With the second version, return (returned - due).days * 50, what does fine return for a book brought back 4 days before its due date?
hint: Count the days with their sign.

prompt: Match each way to green to the situation it fits.

pairs.right: You are unsure what the general code is
One example does not reveal the generalisation
You know exactly what to type, and are right

prompt: You add a test for a return on the due date and it passes the first time it runs. What does that tell you?

choices.text: That the test is broken and must be deleted
choices.why: It may be perfectly correct; it just drove no new code. Keep it if the boundary is worth recording.

choices.text: It drove no code, so it was not a TDD step
choices.why: Right. The existing code already covered it; it may stay as documentation of the boundary, not as a step.

choices.text: That the previous step was too small and should have included it
choices.why: Step size is about how much code changes between greens, and this test changed none.

choices.text: That the max() call in fines.py has no effect and can go
choices.why: Zero days gives zero with or without max; the early-return test is what needs it.

prompt: Which change belongs in the refactor step?

choices.text: Naming the 50 as DAILY_FINE
choices.why: Right. Structure and names change, and every test answers as before.

choices.text: Making films cost 100 cents a day instead of 50
choices.why: That is new behaviour: a new test and a new red, on the next turn.

choices.text: Fixing the failing early-return test by adding max()
choices.why: That is the green step: refactoring only starts once every test passes.

prompt: While extracting days_late you reverse the subtraction, and all three tests go red. What does the lesson tell you to do?

choices.text: Read each failure and reason out which sign is right before touching the code
choices.why: Reasoning works, and is slower than undoing a one-line change you know caused it.

choices.text: Undo the edit and redo it
choices.why: Right. The only thing that changed is the cause; going back to green is one undo away.

choices.text: Update the three tests to expect what the new code returns
choices.why: That would make the tests agree with a bug; in a refactor the tests are the fixed point.

choices.text: Make four more moves, then run again to see the whole picture
choices.why: More moves before a run turn one known cause into a puzzle.

prompt: Why not refactor fines.py and test_fines.py in the same move?

choices.text: Because Python cannot reload two modules in one run
choices.why: Each run starts a fresh interpreter, which loads both files.

choices.text: Because unittest only reports one changed file per run
choices.why: unittest knows nothing about which files changed.

choices.text: If both changed and the run is green, nothing checked either change
choices.why: Right. Each side is the check on the other; moving both at once leaves the green with no meaning.

prompt: Why does overdue take today as an argument instead of calling date.today() inside?

choices.text: date.today() is too slow to call once per loan
choices.why: Speed was never the issue; it returns in microseconds.

choices.text: A test has to choose the day, or its verdict changes with the calendar
choices.why: Right. A test passing on 20 March would fail on 1 April; the argument lets the test fix the day.

choices.text: So the reminders can be sent for dates in the past
choices.why: Production passes the real date; the argument exists for the caller that is a test.

choices.text: Python forbids reading the clock inside a list comprehension
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; it would just make the function untestable without patching.

prompt: Which changes did writing the tests first push into reminders.py? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The clock became an argument
choices.why: Right: today is passed in.

choices.text: The decision split from the sending
choices.why: Right: overdue is pure, and remind is a thin effect around it.

choices.text: The sender is passed in as a function
choices.why: Right: send is injected, a lambda in the test and the mail server in production.

choices.text: An interface was added in front of overdue so a test could replace it
choices.why: overdue takes a list and a date and calls nothing; it needed no injection, and adding one would be the damage the section warns about.

prompt: Which of these is test-induced design damage rather than a healthy pressure from the tests?

choices.text: Passing the clock into a function that decides what is overdue
choices.why: The clock is genuinely awkward in a test; injecting it is the counterweight the section recommends.

choices.text: A FineCalculator interface with one implementation, added only for a test to swap the arithmetic
choices.why: Right. Arithmetic is cheap and deterministic; an interface in front of it adds indirection for the tests alone.

choices.text: Passing the mail sender into remind
choices.why: The network is one of the awkward things worth injecting.

prompt: remind calls notifier.send, but the real Notifier only has deliver. Why is the bare Mock() test green?

choices.text: A bare Mock() creates any attribute the code asks it for
choices.why: Right. The test checked remind against its own assumption, not against Notifier.

choices.text: Mock() copies the methods of the class it replaces, including old names
choices.why: A bare Mock knows no class at all; that is what spec= adds.

choices.text: unittest skips assertions on methods that do not exist
choices.why: The assertion ran and passed, because send was called on the mock.

prompt: Match each double to what it checks.

pairs.right: That each attribute exists on Notifier
Attributes, and the arguments of each call

pairs.left: a lambda appending to a list
pairs.right: Only what the test reads back afterwards

prompt: Which assertion is most likely to break on a harmless refactor?

choices.text: send was called once with the overdue member's address
choices.why: Sending is a command with an effect somebody cares about; asserting it checks behaviour.

choices.text: remind returned 1 for one overdue loan
choices.why: A result is what state-based tests check, and a refactor keeps it.

choices.text: A catalogue lookup was called exactly twice
choices.why: Right. A query's call count is how the code works today; caching or batching it changes the count and nothing else.

choices.text: The message text was "'Dom Casmurro' was due on 2026-03-16"
choices.why: The text is what the member reads; changing it is a change of behaviour, not a refactor.

prompt: What did Nagappan and colleagues report in 2008 for four teams at Microsoft and IBM?

choices.text: Fewer defects and shorter development time, both by about half
choices.why: Defects fell, but development took longer by the managers' estimates, not shorter.

choices.text: Defect density down 40 to 90 per cent, time up 15 to 35
choices.why: Right. A large quality gain bought with extra time, which is why the trade is argued about.

choices.text: No measurable difference in defects, and no change in time
choices.why: Some student studies found little effect; this industrial one found a large drop in defects.

prompt: Fucci and colleagues (2017) looked for what explained differences in quality and productivity among professionals. What did they find?

choices.text: Writing the test before the code
choices.why: The order turned out not to explain the differences.

choices.text: The number of tests each person had written by the end of the task
choices.why: The study looked at the process, and the rhythm of steps was what mattered.

choices.text: Working in short, steady steps
choices.why: Right. Granularity and steadiness explained more than test-first order did.

choices.text: Using mocks for every collaborator from the outset
choices.why: Mocking style was not what the study measured.

prompt: You must find out whether the library's old barcode scanner can be read from Python at all. How does the lesson suggest you start?

choices.text: Write a failing test for read_barcode() and make it pass
choices.why: You do not yet know what read_barcode should return, so there is nothing true to assert.

choices.text: A throwaway spike, then delete it and test-drive the real code
choices.why: Right. The question is what the device does; learn it untested, then start again test-first.

choices.text: Mock the scanner and write the code against the mock
choices.why: A mock of a device you have never read encodes guesses, like the bare Mock that agreed with a missing method.

prompt: A colleague types the full fine formula with max() straight away and the test passes. Was that wrong?

choices.text: Yes: TDD requires a constant first
choices.why: Faking it is one of three strategies, used when unsure; it is not a rule.

choices.text: Yes, because the early-return case now has no test of its own
choices.why: That is a reason to add the test; it does not make the obvious implementation wrong.

choices.text: No, if she knew it; a surprising red would mean smaller steps
choices.why: Right. Obvious implementation is allowed, and the step size drops when the runs start surprising you.

choices.text: No: once the formula is known, tests are not needed for it any more
choices.why: The tests stay; they are what the later refactors rely on.

prompt: A suite of 300 tests goes red in 40 places every time somebody moves a private helper, though no feature changed. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The tests assert how the code works rather than what it does
choices.why: Right. Tests welded to the implementation turn every structural change red, which makes refactoring slower rather than safer.

choices.text: Too few tests: 300 cannot cover a codebase that size
choices.why: Adding more tests of the same kind would add more red, not less.

choices.text: The team skipped the red step when writing them
choices.why: Skipping red risks tests that never fail; these fail too readily, for structural reasons.
